Gubernatorial Former President Goodluck Jonathan
Former President Goodluck Jonathan has warned that growing political intolerance, violence and ethnic divisions could threaten Nigeria’s stability ahead of the 2027 general elections.
Mr Jonathan said political parties and campaign organisations were increasingly adopting the characteristics of cult groups, with young people recruited and used as instruments of violence against political opponents.
He made the remarks on Tuesday at a peace and security conference organised by the Goodluck Jonathan Foundation in Abuja. The conference was themed ‘Safeguarding Peace and Strengthening Social Cohesion in a Competitive Political Environment.’
The former president said he had received concerns from Nigerians and people abroad about the country’s political direction and the possibility of post-election crises.
He identified political intolerance, thuggery and the unwillingness of political actors to accept opposing views as some of the emerging threats to peaceful elections.
“There appears to be an increasing unwillingness among political actors to accommodate opposing views or recognise the legitimate right of others to compete for political power,” he said.
Mr Jonathan added that the recruitment of young people to perpetrate violence had worsened the situation, warning that political campaigns were increasingly taking the form of organised cult activities.

“It’s becoming obvious. We are running political organisations, campaign teams as cult groups,” he said.
Mr Jonathan also expressed concern over conflicting court judgments, particularly decisions issued by courts of coordinate jurisdiction, warning that such controversies could erode public confidence in the judiciary.
Although the courts have the constitutional responsibility to interpret laws and settle disputes, he said contradictory rulings on similar matters could generate tension and encourage citizens to seek alternatives to legal processes.
“We must protect the integrity and independence of our judiciary. When citizens begin to lose faith in the courts and resort to self-help, the consequences can be disastrous,” he said.
He warned that declining confidence in public institutions could create conditions for lawlessness, urging Nigerians to prevent what he described as a possible descent into anarchy.
The former president further cautioned against attempts to exploit ethnic differences for political advantage, saying the 2027 elections should not become a platform for ethnic rivalry at national and state levels.
“Nothing could be more dangerous to our national existence than the deliberate encouragement of ethnic rivalry,” he said.
“We must never allow political ambition to undermine the bonds that hold us together as one nation and in our states.”
Mr Jonathan called for reforms to Nigeria’s political recruitment process, arguing that ethnic, religious and other considerations often prevent competent individuals from emerging as political leaders.
He said Nigerians must pay greater attention to the quality and capacity of candidates seeking elective offices at federal and state levels.
Referring to his recent observation in Lagos, the former president said the country needed to move away from a system that prioritises primordial considerations over leadership capacity.
He urged voters to place national interest and public service above personal and sectional interests when choosing leaders in 2027.
“Our democracy must produce leaders capable of uniting our people and advancing our collective development,” he said.
Also speaking at the conference, Omar Touray, a former president of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) Commission and keynote speaker, said Nigeria’s forthcoming elections would have implications beyond its borders.
Mr Touray said the country’s population, economic influence and diplomatic standing made its democratic performance significant to the wider African continent.
He said the 2027 elections offered Nigeria an opportunity to demonstrate that a diverse society could sustain competitive politics without compromising national unity.
“A peaceful, transparent and credible electoral process in Nigeria would reinforce confidence in democratic governance across the continent,” he said.
Mr Touray also cited Mr Jonathan’s decision to concede defeat in the 2015 presidential election before the final results were announced as an enduring example of democratic statesmanship.
Former Vice President Namadi Sambo, in his remarks, said democracy depended on public trust, mutual respect, credible institutions and citizens’ confidence in the electoral process.
He acknowledged that political competition was necessary in a democracy but warned that it should not come at the expense of national unity and institutional stability.
Mr Sambo said political actors must ensure that their pursuit of power does not weaken the institutions responsible for sustaining democratic governance or threaten the country’s shared identity.
